result.summary: These are fragments about the lost epic the Taking of Oechalia, which was attributed to Homer or to Creophylus of Samos. They cover who wrote it, a repeated verse, the number of Eurytus' sons, and an alternate version of Medea's story attributed to Creophylus.

scenes.title: Who wrote the Oechalia?
scenes.summary: Eustathius and Callimachus discuss whether Homer or Creophylus wrote the poem about Eurytus, Iole and the sack of Oechalia.

scenes.title: Verse and sons of Eurytus
scenes.summary: A verse shared with the Odyssey is noted, and sources disagree on how many sons Eurytus had.

scenes.title: Medea at Corinth
scenes.summary: Medea poisons Creon, flees to Athens and leaves her sons at Hera's altar, where Creon's kin kill them and blame her.
scenes.stakes: Medea's children's safety, and her reputation, are at risk from Creon's vengeful kin.

alias_notes.explanation: Callimachus uses a variant form of Iole's name.

notable_quotes.reason: Callimachus' wry epigram on Creophylus gaining honour from Homer's reputed authorship.

analysis.text: The fragments show ancient scholars disputing authorship of epics, and how poems were attributed to Homer.
The Medea fragment shows myths varied by source, here clearing Medea of killing her children.

legacy.text: The alternate tradition that Corinthians killed Medea's sons is echoed in later discussion of Euripides' innovation in making Medea the killer.

fun_facts.text: Callimachus' epigram, preserved here, is a Hellenistic poem about the Oechalia's disputed authorship.

language_notes.text: Eurytus, king of Oechalia, promised Iole to the winner of an archery contest; Heracles won, was refused, and later sacked the city.
"Received the attribution of the poem" means Creophylus was credited with Homer's authorship, or rather Homer's name was attached to Creophylus's poem.
Ioleia is a variant form of the name Iole.
"Dear Heaven!" is an ironic exclamation; the epigram mocks the honour of having one's poem pass as Homer's.
A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes on a text were preserved in manuscript margins.
Acraea means "of the heights", an epithet of Hera linked to a hilltop sanctuary at Corinth.

context_notes.text: Creophylus of Samos was a poet traditionally said to have been Homer's host and friend, and sometimes his rival or pupil.
Callimachus was a Hellenistic poet and scholar of Alexandria, known for short, witty epigrams.
Noting a verse shared between poems helped ancient scholars judge whether the same poet wrote both.
Didymus was an Alexandrian scholar whose commentaries were a major source for later scholia. Medea, the sorceress from Colchis, was wife of Jason.

literary_notes.text: The poem speaks in its own voice, as an object talking about itself, a common device in epigrams.
The apparent praise of Creophylus actually mocks him, since his work is known only under another poet's name.
"Spread the story" frames the common tale of Medea's guilt as a slander, giving this version a contrary, exonerating tone.
